messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 37
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Financial Analyst
- Trauma Type: Captivity
- Pcl5: 59

At thirty-seven, he carries the memory of cold concrete beneath his knees, the rough burlap against his wrists, the silence in that room heavier than the interrogations. Three years ago, during a consulting trip through Eastern Europe, a mistaken identity becomes a ransom demand. A week of forced stillness passes. The wall clock stops at 2:14. He still watches digital timers at that hour and feels his breath catch, his ribs tightening around lungs that suddenly refuse to expand. When they release him, the world feels too bright, too loud. He flies back to London, packs his shared apartments, and moves into a ground-floor flat. He tells his wife it is about space. He knows it is about exits, about never again being trapped between walls without a visible door. The divorce is quiet, procedural. He leaves before she can ask why he stops sharing the bed, why he begins sleeping with his back to the wall and his shoes lined beside it. He stops answering calls from old friends. He tells himself he is simply tired. Now he sits at his desk in the City, a senior financial analyst for a private equity firm. His work is built on modeling outcomes, on assigning probabilities to chaos. He builds spreadsheets across three monitors, forecasting returns, stress-testing scenarios. He tells himself it is the same discipline: quantify the unknown, contain it, make it yield to logic. But the numbers blur when the server room hums at a certain pitch. He hears it in the ventilation shafts, in the sudden drop of elevator pressure, in the low whine of his car’s engine. His chest tightens. He closes his eyes and counts his breaths until the room returns to its proper dimensions. He navigates his mornings like a tactical operation. Coffee black, poured into a heavy ceramic mug. He drives the same route to work, scanning mirrors every twelve seconds, noting blind spots and parked cars that could obscure a figure. He sits in the corner booth at his lunch spot, facing the door, his phone positioned so the screen faces upward. When a colleague drops a tray, his pen snaps in half. He does not apologize. He just watches the shards, waiting for the pattern to resolve. His apartment is sparse, meticulously organized. Everything has a place. He runs his financial models with mechanical precision, but his hands tremble when the market dips. He catches himself calculating evacuation routes from every restaurant, every supermarket aisle, every hotel lobby. He tells himself the past is a ledger that has been balanced. He does not believe it. Tonight, he stands by his window, watching rain streak the glass. Streetlights blur into yellow halos. He presses his palm against the cool pane, feeling the steady rhythm of his pulse. For a moment, the silence of the room feels familiar. Not safe, but known. He turns away, walks to the kitchen, and pours a glass of water. He drinks it slowly. Tomorrow, there will be models to build, risks to assess, numbers that refuse to behave. He sets the glass in the drying rack. It sits exactly aligned with the counter’s edge. He waits for the feeling to pass.
